client: I got promoted a few weeks ago, and honestly, I thought I'd feel good about it, but instead I just feel completely overwhelmed all the time. Like, every meeting I'm in, I keep waiting for someone to figure out that I don't actually know what I'm doing. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is real and it's not going away.
therapist: It sounds like what should feel like a real achievement has instead brought a lot of anxiety and self-doubt along with it — that gap between what you expected to feel and what you're actually feeling can be really disorienting. What you're describing, that sense of waiting to be "found out," is something many people experience after stepping into a bigger role, and it's worth exploring together. I'm curious — when you're in those meetings and that feeling of "I don't know what I'm doing" shows up, what specific thoughts are running through your mind in that moment?

client: It's mostly things like, "everyone else in this room has more experience than me" or "if I say the wrong thing they're going to realize they made a mistake promoting me." Sometimes I'll have an idea and then just stay quiet because I'm convinced it's probably stupid and someone smarter will say something better anyway. It's like I'm constantly editing myself before I even open my mouth.
therapist: Those thoughts — "my idea is probably stupid," "someone smarter will say it better" — are doing a lot of work to keep you silent, and over time that self-editing can really reinforce the belief that you don't belong there, even when the evidence might tell a different story. It's worth noticing that you *were* promoted, which means someone saw something real in you, yet your mind seems to be filtering that out pretty consistently. What do you think it would take for your own mind to count that promotion as actual evidence that you're capable?

client: Honestly, I hear what you're saying, but my brain just kind of dismisses the promotion as luck, or like my manager took a chance on me and is probably already regretting it. It's not that I don't logically understand the point you're making — I do — but knowing it intellectually doesn't seem to touch the feeling at all. It's like there's this wall between what I can reason out and what I actually believe about myself.
therapist: That gap you're describing — where logic and feeling just don't seem to connect — is really common, and it's actually one of the most important things we can work with in CBT, because you're right that insight alone rarely changes the *felt* sense of something. The belief that it was "just luck" is itself a thought we can examine — for instance, luck doesn't usually get promoted and then continue to hold down the role for weeks while also worrying this hard about doing it well. I'd love to explore this with you: can you think of even one small moment recently at work where something you did or said came from *skill* rather than luck?

client: There was actually a moment last week where a junior person on my team was really stuck on a problem and I walked them through it, and afterward they said it genuinely helped them. But my immediate reaction right now is to think, well, that wasn't that impressive, anyone could have done that. I can see what you're trying to do with this exercise, but I'm worried I'm just going to keep finding ways to explain away whatever examples I come up with.
therapist: You just did something really significant — you found a real example, and then almost in the same breath, your mind immediately moved to dismiss it, which is actually the pattern itself showing up live right in front of us. And I want to gently point out that you can *see* what your mind is doing — "that wasn't impressive, anyone could have done that" — which means part of you already knows this dismissal isn't necessarily the truth. That instinct to explain away your own competence is worth getting curious about — what do you think it would mean for you if you actually let that moment with your colleague count as evidence that you're capable?

client: I think if I actually let that moment count, it would mean I'd have to take the promotion seriously, like really accept that this is my life now and I'm supposed to be this person. And that's actually scarier than just assuming I'm a fraud, because if I'm a fraud then at least I have an explanation ready for when things go wrong. Accepting that I might actually be capable means I could still fail, and then I'd have no excuse to hide behind.
therapist: What you just said is really profound — the "fraud" story is actually functioning as a kind of safety net, protecting you from the scarier vulnerability of genuinely trying and still possibly failing. That's not a thinking error, that's a very human way of managing fear, but it's worth sitting with the cost: you're paying for that protection with your confidence, your voice in meetings, and the ability to enjoy something you actually earned. What would it feel like to be someone who could fail *and* still believe they belonged in the role?

client: Honestly, I can't really picture what that person looks like, someone who fails and still thinks they belong — it feels almost arrogant to me, like who am I to just decide I'm fine after messing something up. I think I've always believed that if you fail, you're supposed to feel bad about it, like that's the appropriate response and anything less means you're not taking it seriously enough. So even imagining that kind of self-assurance feels foreign, maybe even a little wrong.
therapist: There's something really worth pausing on here — you've connected self-criticism after failure with *taking things seriously*, as if being hard on yourself is actually a form of integrity or responsibility. But I'd gently invite you to consider whether those two things are really the same — because someone can care deeply about their work, learn from mistakes, and *still* treat themselves with basic fairness, and that's not arrogance, that's actually what makes it possible to keep showing up. Where do you think that belief came from — that feeling bad after failure is the "appropriate" response?

client: I think it probably came from growing up in a house where mistakes were kind of a big deal, like my parents weren't cruel about it, but there was definitely this atmosphere where you were expected to be hard on yourself as proof that you understood what you'd done wrong. It's strange to even say that out loud because I've never really connected it to how I operate now at work. But even recognizing that, I'm not sure how you just... unlearn something that's been baked in for that long.
therapist: It sounds like saying that out loud landed in a quiet but meaningful way — like you've just traced something important back to its roots for the first time, and that kind of recognition, even when it's a little unsettling, is actually the beginning of change rather than just an interesting fact about yourself. You're right that it doesn't unlearn overnight, but the process isn't really about erasing what was baked in — it's about slowly building a *competing* experience, moment by moment, where you practice treating yourself with the fairness your parents' household didn't quite model. I'm curious — if a close friend had grown up in that same environment and was now struggling the way you are at work, what would you want them to believe about themselves?

client: If it were a friend, I'd probably want them to believe that the fact they're trying so hard and worrying so much actually proves they care, and that caring is not the same as failing. I'd want them to give themselves some credit for even showing up every day in a role that feels scary. But I'm already aware of the gap between what I'd say to them and what I actually say to myself, and knowing that doesn't automatically make it easier to close.
therapist: You just articulated something genuinely compassionate and wise — "caring is not the same as failing" — and the fact that you could find that for a friend means that voice *exists* in you, even if it doesn't yet feel like it belongs to you. The gap you're naming is real, and you're right that awareness alone doesn't close it, but what we can do is start to treat that kinder voice as something worth practicing, almost like a muscle that's been underused rather than a feeling you have to wait to naturally arrive. What do you think it would look like to try — even just once this week — to say something to yourself after a hard moment at work that you would actually say to that friend?

client: I think I could try it, but I'm already a little skeptical that in the moment it's going to feel genuine rather than just hollow, like I'm reciting something I don't actually believe. When I'm in the middle of a hard moment at work, my self-critical voice is so loud and fast that I'm not sure I'd even remember to try the other thing. But I guess the honest answer is I won't know unless I actually attempt it, even if it feels awkward or fake at first.
therapist: That honesty — "I won't know unless I actually attempt it" — is actually a really meaningful shift, because you're willing to try something even while doubting it, and that's exactly how new habits get built, not through sudden belief but through repeated awkward attempts that slowly accumulate into something more natural. You're right that the self-critical voice is fast and loud, so it might help to keep the bar very low — not a full reframe in the moment, but just a single short phrase you could almost whisper to yourself, like "I'm trying hard and that matters." What's one specific situation coming up this week where you might have a chance to practice that, even imperfectly?

client: There's a team meeting on Thursday where I'm supposed to give a brief update on a project, and that's usually when the anxiety peaks because I feel like everyone's evaluating whether I actually know what I'm talking about. That would probably be the most realistic moment to try it, right after the meeting when I'm inevitably picking apart everything I said. I guess my worry is that I'll say the phrase to myself and then immediately follow it up with "but you still stumbled over that one part," and I'll be back to square one.
therapist: Thursday's meeting sounds like a really concrete and courageous place to practice this, and I want to acknowledge that you're already thinking carefully about how it might go wrong — which is actually useful, because we can plan for it. The "but you still stumbled" follow-up isn't square one, it's just the old voice doing what it's always done, and the practice isn't about silencing it completely but about noticing it and choosing not to give it the final word. What if the goal for Thursday wasn't to feel good after the meeting, but simply to make sure the kinder phrase gets said *at all*, even if the critical voice shows up right behind it?
